question: Which dataset does this website use?
reply: The website uses OPSD Household Data, version 2020-04-15, and the CoSSMic residential3 household.

question: Is this dataset generated by ChatGPT?
reply: No. The energy counters are real published measurements. The project derives hourly values and produces separate model forecasts.

question: Is our current dataset from Kaggle?
reply: No. This project uses the official OPSD release, not a Kaggle mirror.

question: Where can I download the official dataset?
reply: Official release: https://data.open-power-system-data.org/household_data/2020-04-15/ . Select household_data_60min_singleindex.csv.

question: Which CSV file is used for training?
reply: The source file is household_data_60min_singleindex.csv. Training selects residential3 PV, grid import and grid export counters.

question: Which household is selected?
reply: CoSSMic residential3 in southern Germany. Other households are not combined into this instance.

question: What is the time resolution?
reply: Each derived record covers exactly one hour. It is average power over the interval, not instantaneous power.

question: What period is displayed by this website?
reply: The held-out records run from {first_time} to {last_time}. Gaps remain visible.

question: How many measured intervals and test records are included?
reply: The cleaned series contains {measured_count} valid intervals. This website displays {total_count} held-out forecast targets.

question: What attribution should I use in my report?
reply: Cite Open Power System Data, Data Package Household Data, version 2020-04-15, primary measurements CoSSMic, under CC BY 4.0. Include the official release URL and describe your transformations.

question: What is the selected record time?
reply: The selected observation ends at {selected_time}. Values refer to the preceding one-hour interval.

question: What is solar generation at the selected hour?
reply: Selected hourly-average solar generation: {solar} kW.

question: What is consumption at the selected hour?
reply: Selected derived household consumption: {load} kW.

question: How much power is imported at the selected hour?
reply: The positive part of net grid exchange is {grid_import} kW. This is net hourly import, not gross metered import.

question: How much power is exported at the selected hour?
reply: The negative part of net grid exchange corresponds to {grid_export} kW net export.

question: What is the net grid power?
reply: Selected net grid exchange: {grid} kW. Positive means import; negative means export.

question: Is solar covering the selected load?
reply: Solar covers {current_coverage}% of the selected hourly demand under the no-unmetered-storage assumption.

question: What is the solar surplus at this record?
reply: Selected solar surplus above demand: {surplus} kW, calculated as max(solar - load, 0).

question: What is the solar deficit at this record?
reply: Selected demand not covered by solar: {deficit} kW, calculated as max(load - solar, 0).

question: What is the solar forecast error at this record?
reply: Absolute selected solar forecast error: {solar_error} kW. The forecast was issued at {issued_time}.

question: Summarize the selected energy window.
reply: Across {window_count} valid hourly records: solar {solar_energy} kWh, load {load_energy} kWh, net-import total {import_energy} kWh, net-export total {export_energy} kWh.

question: How much solar energy is in this window?
reply: Selected-interval solar energy totals {solar_energy} kWh. Missing hours are excluded.

question: How much load energy is in this window?
reply: Selected-interval consumption totals {load_energy} kWh.

question: What is the imported energy total?
reply: Sum of positive hourly net grid exchange: {import_energy} kWh. Gross imports within an hour cannot be recovered from this net series.

question: What is the exported energy total?
reply: Sum of negative hourly net grid exchange magnitudes: {export_energy} kWh.

question: What percentage of load is covered by solar?
reply: Solar directly covers {window_coverage}% of selected-interval demand, using sum(min(solar, load))/sum(load).

question: What is the peak solar generation in this window?
reply: Peak selected solar power: {peak_solar} kW at {peak_solar_time}.

question: What is the peak load in this window?
reply: Peak selected load: {peak_load} kW at {peak_load_time}. Source outliers are retained; unusually large values need investigation.

question: What is the average solar power in the window?
reply: The average across the {window_count} selected hourly records is {mean_solar} kW.

question: What is the average load power in the window?
reply: The average across the {window_count} selected hourly records is {mean_load} kW.

question: What is the next-hour forecast?
reply: {next_forecast}

question: What is the next-hour solar prediction?
reply: {next_solar}

question: What is the next-hour load prediction?
reply: {next_load}

question: When was the next-hour prediction issued?
reply: {next_timing}

question: What does one-hour-ahead prediction mean?
reply: Inputs available at the issue time estimate the next hourly target. Its measured target value is used later for evaluation, not as an input.

question: What is the solar prediction interval?
reply: {next_solar_interval}

question: What is the load prediction interval?
reply: {next_load_interval}

question: Are prediction intervals guaranteed?
reply: No. Intervals use validation residuals with nominal 90% coverage. Temporal distribution changes can lower coverage. Actual test coverage is solar {solar_interval_coverage}% and load {load_interval_coverage}%.

question: Why is a next-hour forecast unavailable?
reply: A saved forecast is available only when its issue timestamp equals the selected record. Missing lag or target intervals and the end of the test period can leave no matching estimate.

question: Are these forecasts for today?
reply: No. Predictions correspond to the original historical timestamps, not today or your own installation.

question: Which models were selected?
reply: Solar: {solar_model}. Load: {load_model}. Selection used validation MAE only.

question: What is the solar test MAE?
reply: Solar test mean absolute error: {solar_mae} kW across {total_count} held-out targets.

question: What is the load test MAE?
reply: Load test mean absolute error: {load_mae} kW.

question: What are the test RMSE values?
reply: Solar RMSE: {solar_rmse} kW; load RMSE: {load_rmse} kW. RMSE penalizes large errors more strongly than MAE.

question: How do the models compare with persistence?
reply: Persistence test MAE is solar {solar_baseline} kW and load {load_baseline} kW. Selected models have MAE {solar_mae} and {load_mae} kW respectively.

question: How was the dataset split for training?
reply: Chronological 60/20/20 partitions, with boundary-crossing labels purged: {train_count} training, {validation_count} validation, {total_count} test examples.

question: Which features are used by the models?
reply: Current and 1h/2h/24h lagged solar/load, target-hour sine/cosine, target month and weekday. No future observed target is a feature.

question: Why is load RMSE large?
reply: Large counter-derived source outliers remain in the load observations. They increase squared error strongly. This is a research model, not reliable dispatch control.

question: What is the solar MAE in the current window?
reply: Selected-window solar MAE: {window_solar_mae} kW across {window_count} records. It differs from whole-test MAE.

question: What is the load MAE in the current window?
reply: Selected-window load MAE: {window_load_mae} kW across {window_count} records.

question: How many solar deviations are flagged?
reply: {flag_count} of {window_count} selected records have solar forecast error strictly above {threshold} kW.

question: What is the largest solar error in this window?
reply: Largest absolute solar error: {worst_error} kW at {worst_time}.

question: What is the current anomaly threshold?
reply: The active solar error threshold is {threshold} kW. Change it on Anomalies.

question: Is the selected record flagged?
reply: Selected record flag: {current_flag}. Error {solar_error} kW; threshold {threshold} kW.

question: What percentage of selected records is flagged?
reply: {flag_percentage}% of selected records exceed the solar error threshold.

question: Does an anomaly mean equipment has failed?
reply: No. A forecast deviation can reflect normal variation, imperfect forecasts or data issues. There are no labelled equipment failures in this subset.

question: How do I mark an alert reviewed?
reply: Open Alerts, find the historical review item and click Mark reviewed. The mark is stored in this browser.

question: How do I undo a reviewed alert?
reply: Use the reviewed or all filter in Alerts, then click Undo review.

question: Why do alert counts change during playback?
reply: The selected window moves with playback. Different observations enter or leave it. Threshold changes also change which records qualify.

question: Are alerts live notifications?
reply: No. Alerts are historical review items within the chosen window. They do not send emails, trigger relays or diagnose current equipment.

question: What is the selected energy exposure score?
reply: The energy exposure index is {score}/100: {risk_band}. This is retrospective energy analysis, not a failure probability.

question: What is the selected grid dependence?
reply: The share of load not covered by solar is {dependence}%. Importing power can be normal.

question: How is the exposure score calculated?
reply: Score = round(100 * (0.7 * D + 0.3 * min(E/T,1))), where D is grid dependence, E is absolute solar forecast error, and T is the active error threshold.

question: Where do the risk weights come from?
reply: The 70% dependence and 30% forecast-error weights are illustrative project choices. They are not learned failure weights or numerical PPT requirements.

question: What are the low, moderate and high bands?
reply: Low: below 30; moderate: 30 to 69; high: at least 70. These are illustrative display bands, not certified operating limits.

question: Is the risk score a probability of failure?
reply: No. The score summarizes historical energy dependence and forecast error. It is not calibrated against failure labels.

question: Why can the score be high at night?
reply: With little solar and positive demand, grid dependence can be high. This can be normal night-time operation and does not imply danger.

question: What happens when load is zero?
reply: The dependence term is set to zero to avoid division by zero. The forecast-error term can still contribute.

question: How does changing the threshold affect the score?
reply: A larger positive threshold reduces or preserves the error-severity contribution for a fixed observation. It does not change the 70% dependence term.

question: Can this score predict future faults?
reply: No. It uses the actual historical target observation and has no equipment-failure labels. It is not a future-fault prediction.

question: What is historical playback for?
reply: Playback replays saved historical observations so you can inspect changing energy values, predictions and flags without sensors.

question: How do I start or pause playback?
reply: Use the Play/Pause button in Historical playback. Pausing freezes the selected record for inspection.

question: How do I change playback speed?
reply: Choose 0.5x, 1x or 3x beside the playback slider. This changes display speed, not the measurement interval.

question: How do I jump to a recorded date?
reply: Use Jump to date. The app selects the first available record on or after that date; missing dates are not fabricated.

question: How do I change the analysis window?
reply: Choose 24, 48 or 168 records in Window. These are available records, not necessarily continuous clock hours.

question: Does playback retrain the AI model?
reply: No. It changes which saved observation and forecast are displayed. Retraining is a separate Python process.

question: How do I open or close the sliding menu?
reply: Use the menu button near the top of the page. On small screens the menu slides over the page; select a section, press Escape or tap the backdrop to close it.

question: How do I enable dark mode?
reply: Choose Dark mode in the theme selector. Your theme preference is saved in this browser.

question: What happens at the end of playback?
reply: Playback stops at the last record. Press Play again to restart from the first record.

question: How do I compare predictions with actual values?
reply: Open AI Prediction. Solid lines show observations and dashed lines show forecasts aligned to target time. Hover on charts to inspect values.

question: How do I export the selected records?
reply: Click Export window CSV above the page content. The CSV contains selected timestamps, observations and saved forecast values.

question: How do I download the analysis report?
reply: Click Download report to save a JSON snapshot with the selected record, window metrics, energy exposure and model results.

question: How do I export the whole test dataset?
reply: Open System Status and select Download full held-out measurements CSV.

question: How do I start the website in VS Code?
reply: Open the extracted microgrid-updated folder, open a terminal, run python backend/server.py and browse to http://localhost:8000.

question: What should I do if port 8000 is busy?
reply: Run python backend/server.py --port 8001, then open http://localhost:8001. Keep that terminal running.

question: Do I need to install Node to view the website?
reply: No. The ZIP contains a prebuilt frontend. Python 3.10+ serves it. Node is needed only to edit and rebuild the frontend.

question: Where are the saved predictions stored?
reply: backend/data/holdout.json contains observations, forecast issue times, predictions and interval bounds. evaluation.json holds model metrics.

question: How do I retrain using the original CSV?
reply: Install backend/requirements.txt, then run python backend/prepare_real_data.py followed by the path to household_data_60min_singleindex.csv. Restart the server after completion.

question: How do I download this chat conversation?
reply: Use Export chat in Chat Assistant. It downloads the visible conversation with each stored dataset context.

question: Where can I find all 100 supported questions?
reply: Open the Question bank in Chat Assistant, search or select a category, then click a question to ask it. The same 100 questions are supplied in the PDF.

question: Do I need physical sensors for this website?
reply: No. This edition reads bundled historical data. Physical sensors are not required.

question: Can you show battery state of charge?
reply: No battery SOC is measured in the selected residential3 subset. The website does not invent it.

question: Can you show temperature or irradiance?
reply: No. Temperature and irradiance are not included in the selected data and cannot be recovered reliably from power alone.

question: Can you show voltage and current?
reply: No. The selected columns are energy counters; voltage and current measurements are absent.

question: Are readings instantaneous or hourly averages?
reply: Displayed kW values are averages derived from differences between hourly cumulative energy counters.

question: What is the difference between kW and kWh?
reply: kW measures power; kWh measures energy. Average kW multiplied by interval hours gives kWh.

question: Why are some times missing from the charts?
reply: Intervals with missing, interpolated or invalid selected counters are excluded. Required lag/target availability also limits held-out examples.

question: Can this website control a battery or grid switch?
reply: No. It is an analysis application and does not actuate hardware, relays or dispatch equipment.

question: Does the chatbot use ChatGPT or an external LLM?
reply: No. This offline assistant matches supported questions and computes answers from selected data. It is not an open-ended generative language model.

question: Can you guarantee perfect predictions?
reply: No. Forecast errors and empirical interval coverage are displayed. Results apply to this historical household and do not guarantee performance on another system.
